title: Religious Foundations — Traditions, Texts, Gods, Esotericism and Societal Coupling
purpose: Build a comparative religious layer above the World tree without changing the canonical ten-level Frame. Separate traditions, texts, institutions, doctrines, denominations, pantheons/deities, esoteric traditions and country-level religious composition so relationships can be expanded without collapsing distinct categories.

method.rule: Do not treat all religions as equivalent systems or force a single genealogy. Record self-understanding, historical scholarship and project interpretation separately.
method.dates: Ancient traditions receive approximate emergence periods rather than invented foundation years. Institutional foundation dates are recorded separately where useful.
method.religious_composition: Country couplings describe demographic or institutional presence, not the belief of every citizen.
method.esotericism: Esoteric material is indexed as a historical or interpretive layer; inclusion does not imply supernatural claims are empirically verified.

traditions.name: Judaism
traditions.foundation_period: Ancient Israelite religion; Jewish tradition traces covenantal origins through Abraham, Moses and Sinai; historical development spans the 1st millennium BCE and earlier
relations_to_other_traditions: parent tradition for Christianity's scriptural inheritance
historical and theological relationship with Islam as an Abrahamic tradition
shared ancient Near Eastern context with other Levantine traditions
secondary_source_leads: academic histories of ancient Israel and rabbinic Judaism
open_questions: How should biblical, rabbinic, mystical and modern denominational layers be separated in the graph?
Which institutions carry which theological authorities today?
How do country-level Jewish populations map onto denominations and institutions?

traditions.name: Christianity
traditions.foundation_period: 1st century CE; centered historically on Jesus of Nazareth and the early Jesus movement
core_doctrines: Jesus Christ as Messiah and Son of God
rituals: confession in traditions that practice it
ethics_law: varied church law and moral theology
esoteric_traditions: gnostic traditions as historical comparative material
relations_to_other_traditions: inherits Jewish scriptures
historically develops from the Second Temple Jewish environment
Islam recognizes Jesus and earlier prophets while rejecting mainstream Christian Trinitarian/Incarnation theology
Christianity has extensive historical interaction with Greco-Roman philosophy and religions
primary_source_leads: Orthodox and Anglican primary liturgical texts
secondary_source_leads: Oxford Dictionary of the Christian Church
open_questions: How should denomination, rite, jurisdiction and theology be represented separately?
Which Christian institutions control which assets and educational networks?
How does historical Christianity couple to European state formation without reducing theology to politics?

traditions.name: Islam
traditions.foundation_period: 7th century CE; Qur'anic revelation associated with Muhammad in Arabia and the formation of the early Muslim community
ethics_law: Sharia as a broad religious-legal tradition
institutions: state religious ministries in some countries
deities_or_divine_conceptions: angels and jinn as created beings
relations_to_other_traditions: recognizes Abraham, Moses, David and Jesus as prophets in Islamic theology
shares monotheistic Abrahamic heritage with Judaism and Christianity
historically interacted with Zoroastrian, Christian, Jewish, Greek philosophical and South Asian traditions
open_questions: How do legal schools map onto states and contemporary institutions?
Where do Sufi networks cross national borders?
How should Sunni/Shia diversity be represented without treating either as monolithic?

traditions.name: Hindu traditions
traditions.foundation_period: Long-duration family of traditions developing from Vedic religion and later Indian religious/philosophical traditions; no single founder or universally accepted foundation date
foundational_texts: Agamas and Tantras in relevant traditions
rituals: yoga and meditation in relevant traditions
deities_or_divine_conceptions: Brahman as ultimate reality in several philosophical systems
relations_to_other_traditions: shares historical South Asian environment with Buddhism, Jainism and Sikhism
has philosophical and historical interactions with Zoroastrian, Islamic and Christian communities
open_questions: How should a non-creedal family of traditions be represented without forcing a church-like structure?
How do regional temple networks map to modern states and diaspora communities?
How should philosophical schools and devotional traditions connect to deity nodes?

traditions.name: Buddhism
traditions.foundation_period: 5th–4th centuries BCE, associated with Siddhartha Gautama/Buddha and the early Buddhist community
deities_or_divine_conceptions: Buddha as awakened teacher rather than creator god
eschatology: future Buddha Maitreya in many traditions
relations_to_other_traditions: arose within the South Asian religious environment
interacted with Hindu philosophical traditions
interacted with East Asian religions and local cosmologies
open_questions: How should monastic lineage, national institutions and philosophical schools be linked?
Which esoteric systems have direct textual lineages versus later interpretations?

traditions.name: Sikhism
traditions.foundation_period: 15th century CE, Punjab; associated with Guru Nanak and the succession of Sikh Gurus
foundational_texts: Dasam Granth in traditions that recognize it
deities_or_divine_conceptions: ten Gurus as historical spiritual teachers, not gods
cosmology: karma and rebirth in Sikh theology
relations_to_other_traditions: emerged in the Punjab religious environment of Hindu and Islamic traditions
distinct theological identity despite shared regional vocabulary
open_questions: How should diaspora institutions be connected to Punjab institutions?
How do gurdwaras function as religious, social and economic institutions?

traditions.name: Jainism
traditions.foundation_period: Ancient South Asian tradition; historical Jain tradition strongly associated with Mahavira in the 6th century BCE, while Jain tradition recognizes a much longer succession of Tirthankaras
deities_or_divine_conceptions: devas as non-creator beings in Jain cosmology
cosmology: karma as subtle matter in Jain metaphysics
eschatology: liberation from karmic bondage and rebirth
relations_to_other_traditions: shares South Asian philosophical environment with Hindu and Buddhist traditions
distinct doctrine of jiva, nonviolence and anekantavada
open_questions: How do Jain ethical principles connect to modern environmental and economic behaviour?
How should ancient cosmology and modern institutional life be separated in the graph?

traditions.name: Zoroastrianism
traditions.foundation_period: Ancient Iranian religion associated with Zarathustra/Zoroaster; date remains debated, with proposals ranging broadly in the 2nd–1st millennium BCE
deities_or_divine_conceptions: Angra Mainyu/Ahriman in later theological formulations
esoteric_traditions: later Iranian mystical and philosophical interpretations
relations_to_other_traditions: deeply connected to ancient Iranian religious history
historically interacted with Judaism, Christianity and Islam under Persian empires
possible influence on later religious concepts is debated and must be sourced rather than assumed
open_questions: Which concepts can be historically demonstrated as influences on later religions?
How did Zoroastrian institutions transform after the Islamic conquest of Iran?

traditions.name: Daoism/Taoism
traditions.foundation_period: Ancient Chinese religious and philosophical traditions; philosophical texts associated with Laozi and Zhuangzi; organized religious Daoism develops later
deities_or_divine_conceptions: Dao as ultimate principle rather than a simple creator-god
relations_to_other_traditions: interacts historically with Confucianism and Buddhism
embedded in Chinese local religious systems
open_questions: How should philosophical Daoism and organized Daoist religion be separated and linked?
How do temple networks couple to local governance and culture?

traditions.name: Shinto
traditions.foundation_period: Ancient Japanese indigenous religious traditions; institutional distinction from Buddhism develops over many centuries and is reshaped in the modern period
denominations_or_schools: State Shinto as a historical political formation
eschatology: varied and less centralized than Abrahamic eschatologies
relations_to_other_traditions: deep historical interaction with Buddhism
interaction with Daoist and Chinese cosmological concepts
modern separation from Buddhism shaped by Meiji policy
open_questions: How should kami, shrine, locality and political history be connected?
How should premodern shrine-Buddhist syncretism be represented?

traditions.name: Satanism
traditions.foundation_period: Modern umbrella term with multiple unrelated historical and contemporary movements; important distinction between literary/anti-Christian uses of Satan and organized modern Satanist religions
foundational_texts: The Satanic Bible for Church of Satan tradition
The Satanic Scriptures and other modern movement texts
historical anti-Christian/literary sources as context rather than scripture
core_doctrines: often individualism, symbolism, autonomy or secular naturalism in modern organized forms
some theistic Satanist groups treat Satan as a real deity or spiritual being
ethics_law: varies strongly by organization and individual tradition
deities_or_divine_conceptions: Satan as symbol in some traditions
Satan as deity or spiritual being in some theistic traditions
cosmology: varies from explicitly atheistic symbolism to supernatural cosmologies
sacred_places: movement-dependent; generally no universal sacred geography
relations_to_other_traditions: defined in some forms through critique or inversion of Christianity
borrows terminology from Western occultism and Romantic/Literary Satanism
must not be collapsed into historical Christian demonology
primary_source_leads: official publications of specific Satanist organizations
secondary_source_leads: religion scholarship on new religious movements
open_questions: Which Satanism is being represented?
What distinguishes symbolic, atheistic, occult and theistic forms?
How should historical accusations of Satanism be separated from self-identifying movements?

important_missing_traditions_for_next_ro: Juche as a political-religious ideology requiring separate treatment

pantheon_layer.purpose: Pantheons are deity/being collections attached to traditions. They are not interchangeable with religions and should not be treated as evidence that two traditions share theology merely because names or archetypes resemble one another.

pantheons.name: Greco-Roman Pantheon
pantheons.period: Bronze Age Greek roots; classical Greek religion; Roman adaptation and transformation

pantheons.name: Norse Pantheon
pantheons.period: Iron Age and Viking Age sources; older Germanic roots

pantheons.name: Ancient Egyptian Pantheons
pantheons.period: 3rd millennium BCE onward through late antiquity

pantheons.name: Mesopotamian Pantheons
pantheons.tradition_context: Sumerian, Akkadian, Babylonian and Assyrian religious traditions
gods: Tiamat as a mythic primordial figure

pantheons.name: Hindu Divine Traditions
pantheons.period: Vedic period onward; transformed across millennia

pantheons.name: Christian Divine Persons and Spiritual Beings
pantheons.note: Christian theology is monotheistic and Trinitarian in mainstream Nicene traditions; angels and demons are created beings, not gods.

pantheons.name: Islamic Divine and Unseen Beings
pantheons.note: Islamic theology is strictly monotheistic; prophets, angels and jinn are not gods.

pantheons.name: Jewish Divine and Heavenly Beings
other_beings: Satan as an evolving theological figure
Shekhinah as a divine-presence concept in later Judaism
pantheons.note: Jewish theology is monotheistic; heavenly beings are not independent gods.

special_comparative_nodes.description: Titan associated in Greek myth with bearing the heavens; later traditions and modern metaphor use Atlas as an image of cosmic support/burden.
Titan and father of Zeus in Greek mythology; Roman Saturn is a related Roman identification, but the traditions should remain historically distinct.
Major Norse god associated with wisdom, knowledge, poetry, magic, war and the dead; central to the surviving Old Norse mythic corpus.
Central figure of Christianity; mainstream Nicene Christianity identifies Jesus with the incarnate Son within the Trinity. Other traditions interpret Jesus differently.

A highly variable figure whose meaning changes across Jewish, Christian, Islamic and modern Satanist contexts; the graph must preserve these distinct meanings rather than assume one continuous character.

religion_to_society_model.description: The key coupling is not religion = country. The useful chain is belief -> text -> interpretation -> institution -> ritual -> law/ethics -> family/community -> education -> political history -> economic assets -> national composition.

country_coupling_seed.research_note: Map constitutional church status, Folkekirken, religious demographics, immigrant/diaspora institutions and religious property separately.

Map immigration, Indigenous traditions, denominational institutions and provincial differences.
Separate England/Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland where constitutional and institutional structures differ.
Map the national church, newer religious communities and changing affiliation.
Separate demographic identification, constitutional structure and institutional recognition.

research_questions: Which religious foundations are genuinely genealogically related, and which merely share motifs?
Which texts are foundational, which are interpretive, and which are later esoteric developments?
How do denominations branch from foundational traditions?
How do religious institutions map onto land, buildings, schools, charities, media and financial assets?
Which countries have constitutional establishment, neutrality, recognition or restriction of particular religions?
How do migration and diaspora networks transmit traditions across borders?
Where do religious traditions cooperate institutionally despite theological disagreement?
Where do religious laws intersect with civil law and family law?
How do sacred places create geographic networks of pilgrimage, money and identity?
Which modern esoteric movements derive demonstrably from older traditions, and which are later reconstructions?
How should gods, angels, demons, saints, ancestors, spirits and philosophical principles be typed so they are not falsely treated as the same category?
How does a society's religious composition relate to education, family formation, political institutions and social trust without assuming simple causation?
